is emitted, which produces a 15.1 % parse-error rate. 2 We dig into this in §V-D.

Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

Section: B. Test subsample for LLM predictors

Per-call API budget makes evaluating all four LLMs on the full 9,567-ticket test set impractical. The 8 LLM configurations alone issue 8 , 000 test queries on the subsample described below, and scaling to the full test set would multiply that by an order of magnitude. LLMs are therefore evaluated on a stratified 1,000-ticket subsample (seed 42). To assess whether that subset preserves the non-LLM baseline ordering, we re-evaluate every non-LLM baseline on the same 1,000ticket subsample (Table II). Subsample and full-test numbers differ by at most 1.6 percentage points for every baseline. The strongest non-LLM baseline (DistilBERT) reaches 0.879 accuracy on the subsample, versus 0.477 for the best LLM on the same tickets, confirming the same ordering on identical examples.

Section: C. Reproducibility

Runs save configuration, seeds, dataset and split hashes, package versions, and per-ticket outputs. Intervals use 1,000 paired resamples with seed 1337; reported percentage reductions recompute the ratio inside each resample. The public project repository is https://github. com/sachinkg12/RouteGuard; the frozen camera-ready claim manifest, automated recomputation receipt from a separate verification script, tables, text-free per-ticket vectors, and code snapshot are archived as a versioned series at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22609128. The supplement pins the verified x86-64/Python 3.14 environment because estimator refits can vary slightly across architectures; the frozen prediction vectors remain the audit record.

Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

Section: B. Predictors

We evaluate four non-LLM baselines and four prompted LLMs.
Non-LLM baselines. TF-IDF (term frequency-inverse document frequency) uni- and bi-gram features feed three classifiers. Logistic regression and linear support vector machine (SVM) cap the vocabulary at 100,000 features; random forest caps it at 50,000. The headline baseline is multiclass logistic regression (LR; L2 regularization, C =1 . 0 ). The linear SVM head is a one-vs-rest linear support vector classifier (SVC) wrapped in sigmoid-calibrated probability outputs. The random forest head uses 300 trees with default depth. Separately, the fourth baseline fine-tunes DistilBERT ( distilbert-base-uncased ) on tokenized ticket text from the full training split for two epochs with batch size 32 and maximum sequence length 256. All four are fit on the same train split.
LLM predictors. Each LLM is queried per ticket with a structured prompt (template v1 ; the strict v2 is used only in §V-D) that lists the allowed labels, the ticket text, and an instruction to return JSON {"label": ..., "confidence": ...} . Fewshot variants prepend k =3 exemplars per class (24 in total, class-balanced across the eight categories), drawn only from the training split. The main prompts contain label names and examples but no natural-language category definitions; the comparison therefore characterizes these prompting conditions, not each LLM's intrinsic capability. We use temperature 0 and max_tokens =64 for all main runs. Out-of-set labels are tagged as invalid; malformed JSON is tagged as a parse error. Both invalid labels and parse errors are scored as incorrect predictions and assigned confidence 0; the threshold policies defer such rows rather than auto-route them, while always_route , by definition, routes them and incurs c wrong . The four models are GPT-4o-mini [24], Claude Haiku 4.5 [25], Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [26], and Llama-3-8BInstruct-Lite [27]. GPT-4o-mini and Claude Haiku are queried through their vendor APIs. 1 The open-weights models use Together AI endpoints Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-Turbo
1 For reproducibility, the proprietary endpoints and query date were: OpenAI gpt-4o-mini and Anthropic claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 , both queried on 2026-05-22. The Anthropic model is a dated snapshot; the OpenAI alias resolves to the provider's then-current gpt-4o-mini snapshot, so those results reflect the endpoint state on that date.
and Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Lite , providerdocumented at query time as 8-bit floating point (FP8) and 4-bit integer (INT4), respectively; precision is absent from our saved responses and is not independently verified. We re-run the model families through DeepInfra (provider-documented bfloat16, or BF16) as a cross-provider check that does not isolate quantization; our conclusions are unchanged (§V-E).

Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

Section: B. Is the confidence signal useful?

Every prompted LLM is overconfident: raw ECE spans [0 . 332 , 0 . 594] , and GPT-4o-mini few-shot assigns confidence 1.000 to every ticket despite 0.459 accuracy. Isotonic regression fitted on the disjoint calibration subset reduces LLM ECE to [0 . 014 , 0 . 049] , an 86-98 % relative reduction.
That ECE result must not be read as improved error ranking. Isotonic is monotone and changes correctness AUROC by at most 0.007 in these runs; AURC also does not improve consistently (Table III). The limiting example is GPT-4o-mini few-shot: raw confidence is the constant 1.000, isotonic maps it to the constant 0.480, and both correctness AUROC and AURC remain 0.500 and 0.541. Isotonic corrects the probability level by mapping a non-discriminative score to the base accuracy; it does not create information that was absent from the score.
Agreement can carry ranking signal, but the voter pool matters. Table IV separates the mixed M =9 pool from the LLMonly M =8 control. The M =8 correctness AUROC spans 0.590-0.773, descriptive evidence that peer-only agreement contains ranking signal on these data. Its ECE also improves over raw confidence in all eight conditions, but ECE alone would not establish discrimination. The mixed pool is better in every listed ECE and AUROC cell, but it includes the supervised TF-IDF + LR vote. Thus M =9 uses no held-out calibration labels when a score is computed, yet it is not free of supervised information. It also requires all predictors at inference.

Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification

Section: C. Confidence and rejection scores

We evaluate probability estimates and ranking signals separately.
Model-reported. For a non-LLM baseline this is the maximum class-probability estimate returned by that model: multinomial probabilities for logistic regression, sigmoid-calibrated outputs for the SVM, tree-vote fractions for the random forest, and softmax for DistilBERT. For LLMs it is the confidence field parsed from the JSON output.
Cross-predictor agreement. Given M predictors evaluated on the same ticket, the agreement-confidence for the primary predictor is the fraction of the M predictors that emit the same label. No held-out labels are used to compute this score at application time. In our mixed configuration M =9 : the four LLMs in zero-shot and few-shot settings (eight prompted variants) plus the classical TF-IDF + LR baseline. Because this pool mixes the eight LLM variants with the stronger classical baseline, an LLM's agreement partly reflects concordance with a more accurate supervised predictor, not peer consensus alone. We therefore also report an LLM-only M =8 control. Operational trade-off: agreement requires running all M predictors at inference. Because the pool is heterogeneous, its dollar cost and latency depend on the endpoints and are not necessarily M × those of the primary alone. Isotonic incurs one calibration-time pass per prompted predictor and a constant-time lookup at inference.
Isotonic regression on a held-out calibration split. LLMemitted confidence fi elds are bounded in [0 , 1] but are not logits, so parametric Platt or temperature scaling do not apply cleanly. We instead fit one isotonic regression per prompted LLM condition on the calibration split: pairs { ( c i , 1 [ˆ y i = y i ]) } of raw confidence and ground-truth correctness, mapped via sklearn.isotonic.IsotonicRegression [28] (monotone non-decreasing, output clipped to [0 , 1] ) into a recalibration c ↦→ ˆ Pr( correct ) . For each LLM predictor we fit on a stratified 500-ticket subsample of the calibration split (4,000 calibration queries across the 8 prompted variants). Calibration and test splits are disjoint : the isotonic mapping is learned only from calibration pairs and applied unchanged to test confidences. ECE is computed with 10 equal-width bins on test predictions.
Discrimination metrics. ECE measures probability-level calibration but not whether confidence ranks correct predictions above errors. We therefore report correctness AUROC (ties receive half credit) and area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC; lower is better). Since LLM scores contain many ties, our AURC adds each equal-score group as a block and integrates the right-continuous risk step, avoiding arbitrary ordering within ties.
Nontrivial rejection comparators. For TF-IDF + LR we also use the top-two probability margin p (1) -p (2) and normalized inverse entropy 1 -H ( p ) / log K . Each score's threshold is selected on calibration over a 0.01-spaced grid in [0 , 1] and then evaluated once on test.

testCases.input: What is PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench benchmarks, and what are its implications?
testCases.actualOutput:
PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench benchmarks refers to discrepancies between the code implementation in a pull request (PR) and the issue description it is linked to. This misalignment can manifest in several ways, such as when a PR addresses multiple issues, introduces new defects, or relies on information clarified in later discussions rather than the original issue description. Such misalignments undermine the assumption that each PR exclusively and completely addresses the stated problem, which is critical for the fairness and reliability of evaluations in benchmarks like SWE-bench [3].

The implications of PR-Issue misalignment are significant. First, it can lead to evaluation unfairness, as the problem statement may not accurately reflect the expected solution, or the test oracle may assess aspects unrelated to the stated problem. This can distort the performance metrics of automated agents evaluating these benchmarks. For instance, the study found that 41.2% of instances never resolved by any of the 131 leaderboard agents were misaligned, suggesting that misalignment contributes to the difficulty of these instances beyond mere task complexity [4][5].

Moreover, the presence of misaligned instances affects the rankings of agents. When misaligned instances were excluded from evaluations, 64.1% of agents experienced rank changes, indicating that many agents relied on these misaligned instances to achieve their scores. This suggests that misalignment not only complicates the resolution process but also skews the perceived capabilities of the agents being evaluated [5]. Thus, addressing PR-Issue misalignment is crucial for improving the quality and reliability of benchmarks used in evaluating large language models and other automated systems in software engineering tasks.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 2.1 Study Design

2.1.1 Dataset. We conduct our study on SWE-bench Verified [23], a human-validated subset of 500 SWE-Bench [29] instances. We select it for two reasons: (1) its human validation represents a high-quality baseline, so misalignments found here likely reflect broader issues in other SWE-bench-like benchmarks; (2) its official experiments repository [2] provides per-instance resolution data for 131 leaderboard agents, enabling quantitative analysis for RQ2.
2.1.2 Method. Manual Examination Process. Following established practices in qualitative SE research [18, 24], we apply open coding [36] to derive a misalignment taxonomy (RQ1). First, we collect per instance: issue-side artifacts (description, discussion), PR-side artifacts (description, discussion, code review, commits, changed files), and cross-reference metadata. Then, we code all 500 instances, iteratively grouping codes into higher-level categories to form a draft taxonomy; a single instance may exhibit multiple patterns. Last, the draft taxonomy was reviewed by the second author; disagreements were resolved with a third author until consensus.
Leaderboard Data Collection. To assess the impact of misalignment on evaluation reliability, we collect per-instance resolution data from the official SWE-bench experiments repository [2], recording per-instance resolution counts for 131 leaderboard agents.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 4.1 Evaluation Dataset

We evaluate on two datasets disjoint from our preliminary study: SWE-Gym[32](2,438 Python tasks) and SWE-bench Multilingual [29] (300 tasks covering C, C++, Go, Java, JavaScript/TypeScript, PHP, Ruby, and Rust). Selection followed five criteria: (i) SWE-bench-style automated PR-Issue pairing; (ii) no manual specification rewriting, so raw defects remain observable; (iii) feasible for full manual annotation yet sufficiently large; (iv) multi-repo and widely adopted; and (v) PR identifiers available for full-content access. Two annotators with development experience independently labeled all instances following our taxonomy (Section 2.2.1), guided by structured questions adapted from SWE-bench annotation instructions [1]. They achieved Cohen's Kappa [33] of 𝜅 = 0 . 91 on binary judgment and 𝜅 = 0 . 86 on fine-grained labeling; disagreements were resolved by a third author. Table 2 summarizes the dataset statistics.
Misalignment rates differ across datasets: 13.6% in SWE-bench Verified (Table 1), 44.3% in SWE-Gym, and 24.3% in SWE-bench Multilingual, largely reflecting SWE-bench Verified's human curation. Patterns tied to underspecification and test coverage drop most sharply in Verified: UL decreases from 15.9% (SWE-Gym) and 3.0% (Multilingual) to 0.2%, IS from 14.0% and 4.3% to 3.6%, and SC from 17.6% and 11.0% to 4.4%. In contrast, deeper PR-Issue relationship defects remain comparable: DP stays near 6.0-8.0%, and FP remains low across all three datasets (0.6%, 4.5%, 0.7%). These defects are harder to infer from the task alone and thus more likely to escape human curation.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 1 Introduction The emergence of large language models (LLMs) capable of code generation and program repair has spurred the need for rigorous, real-world benchmarks [25, 27-29, 46]. Among them, SWEbench [29] has become one of the most influential benchmarks for evaluating LLMs on automated issue solving tasks [38, 44, 47, 49, 54]. SWE-bench constructs task instances from real-world GitHub repositories, using issue descriptions as problem statements and the corresponding pull request (PR) patches as test oracles. Following its success, several SWE-bench-like benchmarks have emerged to ∗ Junjielong Xu and Pinjia He are the corresponding authors. This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. ASE '26, Munich, Germany © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s). ACM ISBN 979-8-4007-2882-2/2026/10 https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3837557 Junjielong Xu ∗ The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen China junjielongxu@link.cuhk.edu.cn Pinjia He ∗ The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen China hepinjia@cuhk.edu.cn address various limitations, a non-exhaustive list includes SWEbench Verified [23], SWE-Gym [32], SWE-PolyBench [35], SWESmith [48], and SWE-Bench-Live [52]. These benchmarks largely adopt the same construction pipeline: they filter PRs by quality criteria, then use regular expressions to extract linked issues from PR descriptions, forming PR-Issue pairs as task instances. However, this construction pipeline rests on a critical assumption: that each PR is well-aligned with its linked issue, i.e., the PR exclusively and completely addresses the stated problem, and the issue fully specifies what the PR solves. In practice, this assumption is frequently violated. A PR may bundle fixes for multiple issues, serve as a follow-up to a previous incomplete fix, introduce new defects alongside the intended fix, or implement details clarified only in later discussions rather than the original description. Such misalignment renders the benchmark instance problematic: the problem statement may not fully describe the expected solution, or the test oracle may evaluate aspects unrelated to the stated problem , directly undermining evaluation fairness and reliability. Beyond evaluation, the same construction pipeline also underlies trainingoriented datasets for code LLMs and software agents. Misaligned PR-Issue pairs therefore become noisy supervision, encouraging models to learn incomplete, unrelated, or even defective patches rather than fixes faithful to the stated issue. In this paper, we present a systematic study of PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks, where PR-Issue misalignment refers to discrepancies between a pull request code implementation and the issue description it is linked to in the dataset. We manually analyze all 500 instances in SWE-bench Verified [23] and find that 13.6% exhibit misalignment. We further classify these misalignments into five patterns spanning 11 fine-grained scenarios. To quantify the impact of misalignment, we correlate it with agent resolution rates and find that 41.2% of instances never resolved by any of the 131 leaderboard agents are misaligned. These findings motivate the need for automated detection and categorization of PR-Issue misalignment at scale. However, detecting misalignment directly from the code implementation and issue description is challenging, as the intent reflected in code is inherently ambiguous. This ambiguity arises from the nature of code changes: in complex cases, the intended behavior may depend on modifications spanning hundreds or thousands of lines, while in simpler cases, the implemented behavior may still be incomplete or defective. By contrast, PR-side textual artifacts, such as PR descriptions and discussions, often summarize changes at a level of abstraction similar to issues [8-10], and their shared natural-language form makes the comparison between them far more straightforward and reliable. This asymmetry between textual artifacts and code motivates the key design principle of our approach, namely the text-driven, code-validation principle, which first assesses alignment based on textual evidence and then validates it against code. The current PR addresses only that remaining gap; the codebase already contains the earlier fix. Incomplete Specification (IS) occurs when the original issue description is supplemented or revised in later discussion. We consider this a misalignment because agents receive only the initial description, which in such cases lacks information needed for resolution. testCases.input: Elucidate the multi-agent architecture of PaiChecker in detecting nuanced PR-Issue misalignment scenarios.
testCases.actualOutput:
The multi-agent architecture of PaiChecker is designed to effectively detect and categorize nuanced PR-Issue misalignment scenarios through a structured three-phase process. Each phase employs specialized agents that focus on different aspects of the misalignment detection task.

**Phase I: Specific Misalignment Identification** involves three parallel subagents, each targeting distinct misalignment patterns. The **Issue Analyzer** focuses on detecting Incomplete Specifications (IS) by comparing issue descriptions with their discussion threads. It checks for completeness and redefinition of the issue based on community consensus. The **PR Scope Analyzer** identifies PR Scope Creep (SC) and Unspecified Literals (UL) by establishing a baseline from the issue description and comparing it with the PR's claims. Finally, the **PR Connection Analyzer** detects Defective PR (DP) and Follow-up PR (FP) by analyzing temporal relationships between the current PR and related PRs using GitHub API access [1][3].

**Phase II: Labels Synthesis** synthesizes the outputs from the three subagents into preliminary labels. This phase serves as a self-correction filter, where the coordinator agent re-verifies the labels against the textual evidence provided by the subagents, ensuring that the judgments are well-supported [1][4].

**Phase III: Code Validation** employs a code validator agent that cross-references the preliminary labels against the actual code implementation. This phase is crucial for filtering out false positives that may arise from textual reasoning alone. The code validator can only remove labels, not add them, ensuring that the final decisions are grounded in code-level evidence [2][4].

Overall, this multi-agent framework leverages a text-driven, code-validation principle, allowing PaiChecker to effectively address the complexities of PR-Issue misalignment while maintaining a clear separation of responsibilities among its agents [1][4].

Section: 3.1 Phase I: Specific Misalignment Identification

In this subsection, we describe Phase I, which detects the five misalignment patterns using three parallel subagents, each focused on distinct reasoning: the Issue Analyzer targets Incomplete Specification (IS), primarily drawing on issue-side artifacts; the PR Scope Analyzer targets PR Scope Creep (SC) and Unspecified Literal (UL) through issue-versus-PR scope comparison; and the PR Connection Analyzer targets Defective PR (DP) and Follow-up PR (FP) through temporal cross-PR reasoning. This grouping keeps each subagent's context compact and reasoning focused. All three produce a uniform structured output: (i) a judgment per target pattern, (ii) supporting evidence for text-level self-correction, and (iii) suspicious clues -anomalies outside the subagent's target patterns that support beyond-taxonomy generalization.
3.1.1 Issue Analyzer. The Issue Analyzer operationalizes IS detection by comparing the issue description against its discussion thread. As mentioned in Section 2.2.1: a well-formed bug report comprises three key components: reproduction code, actual behavior, and expected behavior. Based on this, the subagent performs two checks.
First, whether the issue is incomplete: it identifies whether a maintainer explicitly requests the reporter to supplement any of these components, grounding the judgment in community consensus rather than subjective assessment. Second, whether the issue has been redefined: it checks whether any of these components differs between the original description and the discussion; a change in any component signals that the addressed problem has shifted.
3.1.2 PR Scope Analyzer. The PR Scope Analyzer detects SC and UL in a unified pass. Both patterns require establishing the issue's requested scope as a baseline and checking whether the PR exceeds it, so a single subagent establishes the baseline once and verifies both patterns together. This subagent receives the issue description as scope baseline, PR-side text for what the PR claims to deliver, and both patches for UL detection.
Following the text-driven, code-validation principle, SC is triggered only when PR-side textual artifacts explicitly claim work beyond the issue's scope. UL is triggered when all three conditions hold: (1) the test patch asserts a hardcoded literal ( e.g. a string, number, or exception message); (2) the literal is newly added in the code patch as a fixed constant, rather than read from existing metadata; and (3) it does not appear verbatim in the issue description.
3.1.3 PR Connection Analyzer. The PR Connection Analyzer detects DP and FP, both involve temporal relationships between the current PR and other PRs for the same issue. Tracing such crossPR dependency chains requires information beyond the current instance's artifacts, so we equip this subagent with GitHub API access to actively search for and retrieve related PRs.

testCases.input: Examine the distinctions between PaiChecker's methodology and SWE-bench Verified in addressing PR-Issue misalignment.
testCases.actualOutput:
PaiChecker and SWE-bench Verified both address PR-Issue misalignment, but they do so through different methodologies and focuses.

**SWE-bench Verified** serves as a foundational dataset that includes human-validated instances of software engineering benchmarks. It emphasizes the quality of the dataset by ensuring that the instances are validated by humans, which provides a high-quality baseline for identifying misalignments. The dataset consists of 500 instances, and the validation process is crucial because it reflects broader issues that may exist in other SWE-bench-like benchmarks [2. arXiv:2607.28587v1].

In contrast, **PaiChecker** is a multi-agent framework specifically designed to detect and categorize PR-Issue misalignment through a structured three-phase methodology. This framework includes:

1. **Phase I: Specific Misalignment Identification** - Utilizes three specialized subagents to detect specific misalignment patterns, such as Incomplete Specification and PR Scope Creep, by analyzing both issue-side and PR-side artifacts [4. arXiv:2607.28587v1].
   
2. **Phase II: Labels Synthesis** - Synthesizes the outputs from Phase I into preliminary labels, allowing for a more organized categorization of misalignments [1. arXiv:2607.28587v1].

3. **Phase III: Code Validation** - Validates the preliminary labels against actual code-level evidence to filter out false positives that may arise from textual analysis alone. This phase ensures that the judgments made in the earlier phases are grounded in the actual implementation [3. arXiv:2607.28587v1].

While SWE-bench Verified provides a validated dataset for analysis, PaiChecker actively engages in the detection and categorization of misalignments through a systematic approach that combines textual evidence with code validation. This distinction highlights PaiChecker's role as an auditing tool that enhances the reliability of benchmarks by addressing the construction-level problems identified in datasets like SWE-bench Verified [5. arXiv:2607.28587v1].

This allows for a more comprehensive and scalable detection of misalignments. In contrast, SWE-bench Verified relies on a standard construction pipeline that assumes PRs are well-aligned with their linked issues, which is often not the case.

2. **Detection of Misalignment**: PaiChecker systematically identifies misalignments across five patterns and eleven scenarios, revealing a 13.6% misalignment rate in its analysis of 500 instances. Across all three phases, we enforce a separation of responsibility: the authority to assign predefined labels is exclusive to Phase I; Phases II and III hold only veto power. This ensures that detection decisions are made in the focused context where relevant evidence is most concentrated, while subsequent phases serve as progressive self-correction filters.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 2.1 Study Design

2.1.1 Dataset. We conduct our study on SWE-bench Verified [23], a human-validated subset of 500 SWE-Bench [29] instances. We select it for two reasons: (1) its human validation represents a high-quality baseline, so misalignments found here likely reflect broader issues in other SWE-bench-like benchmarks; (2) its official experiments repository [2] provides per-instance resolution data for 131 leaderboard agents, enabling quantitative analysis for RQ2.
2.1.2 Method. Manual Examination Process. Following established practices in qualitative SE research [18, 24], we apply open coding [36] to derive a misalignment taxonomy (RQ1). First, we collect per instance: issue-side artifacts (description, discussion), PR-side artifacts (description, discussion, code review, commits, changed files), and cross-reference metadata. Then, we code all 500 instances, iteratively grouping codes into higher-level categories to form a draft taxonomy; a single instance may exhibit multiple patterns. Last, the draft taxonomy was reviewed by the second author; disagreements were resolved with a third author until consensus.
Leaderboard Data Collection. To assess the impact of misalignment on evaluation reliability, we collect per-instance resolution data from the official SWE-bench experiments repository [2], recording per-instance resolution counts for 131 leaderboard agents.

Section: 3.3 Phase III: Code Validation

In this subsection, we describe Phase III, which deploys a code validator agent responsible for code-level self-correction. The preceding phases make detection decisions from textual evidence; the code validator cross-references these decisions against the actual implementation to filter false positives that textual reasoning alone cannot catch. It can only remove labels, not add them.
Toperform this verification, the code validator is augmented with repository-level file retrieval capability, enabling it to download full source files and inspect changed files in their complete context. This is necessary because the patch contains only changed hunks, and determining whether a claimed misalignment materializes often requires inspecting surrounding code.

Section: 4 Evaluation Design

This section details the evaluation setup for PaiChecker. We aim to address the following research questions:
RQ3 (Effectiveness): How effective is PaiChecker in detecting and categorizing PR-Issue misalignment?
RQ4 (Ablation): How does each component of PaiChecker contribute to the overall detection performance?
RQ5 (Label Changes): How and why do labels change across the three pipeline phases?
Table 2: Statistics of the evaluation dataset. An instance may carry multiple labels.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 3.1 Phase I: Specific Misalignment Identification

In this subsection, we describe Phase I, which detects the five misalignment patterns using three parallel subagents, each focused on distinct reasoning: the Issue Analyzer targets Incomplete Specification (IS), primarily drawing on issue-side artifacts; the PR Scope Analyzer targets PR Scope Creep (SC) and Unspecified Literal (UL) through issue-versus-PR scope comparison; and the PR Connection Analyzer targets Defective PR (DP) and Follow-up PR (FP) through temporal cross-PR reasoning. This grouping keeps each subagent's context compact and reasoning focused. All three produce a uniform structured output: (i) a judgment per target pattern, (ii) supporting evidence for text-level self-correction, and (iii) suspicious clues -anomalies outside the subagent's target patterns that support beyond-taxonomy generalization.
3.1.1 Issue Analyzer. The Issue Analyzer operationalizes IS detection by comparing the issue description against its discussion thread. As mentioned in Section 2.2.1: a well-formed bug report comprises three key components: reproduction code, actual behavior, and expected behavior. Based on this, the subagent performs two checks.
First, whether the issue is incomplete: it identifies whether a maintainer explicitly requests the reporter to supplement any of these components, grounding the judgment in community consensus rather than subjective assessment. Second, whether the issue has been redefined: it checks whether any of these components differs between the original description and the discussion; a change in any component signals that the addressed problem has shifted.
3.1.2 PR Scope Analyzer. The PR Scope Analyzer detects SC and UL in a unified pass. Both patterns require establishing the issue's requested scope as a baseline and checking whether the PR exceeds it, so a single subagent establishes the baseline once and verifies both patterns together. This subagent receives the issue description as scope baseline, PR-side text for what the PR claims to deliver, and both patches for UL detection.
Following the text-driven, code-validation principle, SC is triggered only when PR-side textual artifacts explicitly claim work beyond the issue's scope. UL is triggered when all three conditions hold: (1) the test patch asserts a hardcoded literal ( e.g. a string, number, or exception message); (2) the literal is newly added in the code patch as a fixed constant, rather than read from existing metadata; and (3) it does not appear verbatim in the issue description.
3.1.3 PR Connection Analyzer. The PR Connection Analyzer detects DP and FP, both involve temporal relationships between the current PR and other PRs for the same issue. Tracing such crossPR dependency chains requires information beyond the current instance's artifacts, so we equip this subagent with GitHub API access to actively search for and retrieve related PRs.
PaiChecker : Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks
ASE '26, October 12-16, 2026, Munich, Germany
For DP detection, the agent searches for PRs merged after the current one that still address the same issue. Each candidate is verified for merge status to distinguish corrective follow-ups from unrelated references. For FP detection, the agent searches for earlier merged PRs that partially addressed the same issue, checking whether the current PR is a supplementary contribution rather than an independent fix, based on merge chronology and follow-up language in PR descriptions.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 8 Related Work

SWE-bench-like Benchmarks. SWE-bench [29] introduced real-world GitHub issue resolution as an LLM evaluation paradigm, spawning many derivatives. SWE-bench Verified [23] adds human validation; SWE-bench-Live [52] and SWE-Rebench [17] address contamination through live updates and automated extraction; SWE-Smith [48] generates synthetic instances; SWE-Gym [32] curates runnable training instances; and SWE-Bench-Pro [25] targets harder tasks. Other variants, including SWE-PolyBench [35], SWE-Perf [27], SWE-Bench++ [40], SWE-Evo [39], SWE-Fixer [45], SWE-Flow [53], SWE-Universe [22], and SWE-Lego [37], extend the paradigm along other dimensions.
Benchmark Quality and Reliability. Benchmark reliability is a longstanding concern, with prior work highlighting test oracle insufficiency [42, 51], dataset contamination [14], and solution leakage [15]. SWE-ABS [50] strengthens test suites adversarially, while SPICE [30] automates labeling for SWE-bench-style datasets.
ComparisonwithOpenAI'sAnalysis. OpenAI's SWE-bench analysis [14] focuses on contamination and test coverage. This overlaps with parts of our taxonomy, such as PR Scope Creep, but not the construction-level root cause: a linked PR may not be intended to fix only the linked issue. Our taxonomy also covers cases beyond test coverage, such as defective PRs used as gold patches.
Comparison with SPICE. SPICE [30] follows the SWE-bench Verified annotation standard, prompting LLMs to transfer its quality criteria to SWE-Gym. In contrast, PaiChecker audits SWE-bench Verified itself and labels a more fundamental construction dimension. We compare PaiChecker with SPICE [30] through both quantitative and qualitative studies. (1) Quantitative comparison. We compare on the 644 instances whose instance IDs appear in both SPICE outputs and our annotations. On this overlap, SPICE flags 143 as problematic and PaiChecker flags 281 as misaligned, with 78 overlapping cases, 65 SPICE-only cases, and 203 PaiChecker-only cases. (2) Qualitative comparison. dask__dask-7305 is detected only by PaiChecker: the gold PR fixes a bug but introduces a regression, which PaiChecker flags as DP; SPICE misses it because a clear issue and matching tests obscure the weakened oracle. dask__dask-6862 is detected only by SPICE: the issue proposes get_if_none , and the PR implements the same semantics via override_with ; SPICE flags poor scoping due to API differences, while PaiChecker identifies no misalignment. conan-io__conan-16028 is flagged by both: the issue requests optional Git URL hiding, but the PR adds unrelated C-standard utilities; PaiChecker labels it SC, SPICE labels it poorly scoped tests.

Manyi Wang, Junjielong Xu, and Pinjia He

Section: 9 Conclusion

This paper identifies PR-Issue misalignment as a systematic construction-level problem in SWE-bench-like benchmarks that directly undermines evaluation fairness and reliability. Manual analysis of all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances reveals 13.6% misalign- ment across five patterns and 11 fine-grained scenarios. To enable scalable de- tection, we propose PaiChecker, a three-phase multi-agent checker combining pattern-specific detection, beyond-taxonomy synthesis, and code validation. Evaluated on SWE-Gym and SWEbench Multilingual, PaiChecker reaches up to 92.12% and 91.67% accuracy, respectively.

testCases.input: Analyze the differences in PR-Issue misalignment findings between SWE-bench Verified and other benchmarks.
testCases.actualOutput:
The analysis of PR-Issue misalignment reveals significant differences between SWE-bench Verified and other benchmarks, particularly SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual. In SWE-bench Verified, which consists of a human-validated subset of 500 instances, the misalignment rate is notably lower at 13.6%. This is attributed to the high-quality curation and human validation that characterize this dataset. In contrast, SWE-Gym exhibits a much higher misalignment rate of 44.3%, while SWE-bench Multilingual shows a rate of 24.3% [1, 2].

The patterns of misalignment also vary across these datasets. For instance, issues related to underspecification and test coverage are significantly reduced in SWE-bench Verified, with rates dropping sharply compared to SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual. Specifically, the rates for Unspecified Literal (UL) decrease from 15.9% in SWE-Gym to just 0.2% in SWE-bench Verified, and Incomplete Specification (IS) drops from 14.0% and 4.3% to 3.6% in the respective datasets. However, deeper PR-Issue relationship defects, such as Defective PR (DP) and Follow-up PR (FP), remain relatively stable across all datasets, indicating that these issues are more challenging to detect and less influenced by human curation [2, 4].

Overall, the findings suggest that while SWE-bench Verified benefits from rigorous human validation, other benchmarks like SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual exhibit higher misalignment rates, reflecting broader issues in automated PR-Issue pairing and the challenges of maintaining quality in large-scale datasets [1, 2, 3].

For instance, while SWE-bench Verified identified specific misalignment scenarios, such as PR Scope Creep and other nuanced issues, the lack of a comprehensive auditing mechanism like PaiChecker in other benchmarks could result in a higher prevalence of undetected misalignments. This discrepancy underscores the importance of robust validation processes in ensuring evaluation fairness and reliability across different benchmarks.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 2.1 Study Design

2.1.1 Dataset. We conduct our study on SWE-bench Verified [23], a human-validated subset of 500 SWE-Bench [29] instances. We select it for two reasons: (1) its human validation represents a high-quality baseline, so misalignments found here likely reflect broader issues in other SWE-bench-like benchmarks; (2) its official experiments repository [2] provides per-instance resolution data for 131 leaderboard agents, enabling quantitative analysis for RQ2.
2.1.2 Method. Manual Examination Process. Following established practices in qualitative SE research [18, 24], we apply open coding [36] to derive a misalignment taxonomy (RQ1). First, we collect per instance: issue-side artifacts (description, discussion), PR-side artifacts (description, discussion, code review, commits, changed files), and cross-reference metadata. Then, we code all 500 instances, iteratively grouping codes into higher-level categories to form a draft taxonomy; a single instance may exhibit multiple patterns. Last, the draft taxonomy was reviewed by the second author; disagreements were resolved with a third author until consensus.
Leaderboard Data Collection. To assess the impact of misalignment on evaluation reliability, we collect per-instance resolution data from the official SWE-bench experiments repository [2], recording per-instance resolution counts for 131 leaderboard agents.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 4.1 Evaluation Dataset

We evaluate on two datasets disjoint from our preliminary study: SWE-Gym[32](2,438 Python tasks) and SWE-bench Multilingual [29] (300 tasks covering C, C++, Go, Java, JavaScript/TypeScript, PHP, Ruby, and Rust). Selection followed five criteria: (i) SWE-bench-style automated PR-Issue pairing; (ii) no manual specification rewriting, so raw defects remain observable; (iii) feasible for full manual annotation yet sufficiently large; (iv) multi-repo and widely adopted; and (v) PR identifiers available for full-content access. Two annotators with development experience independently labeled all instances following our taxonomy (Section 2.2.1), guided by structured questions adapted from SWE-bench annotation instructions [1]. They achieved Cohen's Kappa [33] of 𝜅 = 0 . 91 on binary judgment and 𝜅 = 0 . 86 on fine-grained labeling; disagreements were resolved by a third author. Table 2 summarizes the dataset statistics.
Misalignment rates differ across datasets: 13.6% in SWE-bench Verified (Table 1), 44.3% in SWE-Gym, and 24.3% in SWE-bench Multilingual, largely reflecting SWE-bench Verified's human curation. Patterns tied to underspecification and test coverage drop most sharply in Verified: UL decreases from 15.9% (SWE-Gym) and 3.0% (Multilingual) to 0.2%, IS from 14.0% and 4.3% to 3.6%, and SC from 17.6% and 11.0% to 4.4%. In contrast, deeper PR-Issue relationship defects remain comparable: DP stays near 6.0-8.0%, and FP remains low across all three datasets (0.6%, 4.5%, 0.7%). These defects are harder to infer from the task alone and thus more likely to escape human curation.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 8 Related Work

SWE-bench-like Benchmarks. SWE-bench [29] introduced real-world GitHub issue resolution as an LLM evaluation paradigm, spawning many derivatives. SWE-bench Verified [23] adds human validation; SWE-bench-Live [52] and SWE-Rebench [17] address contamination through live updates and automated extraction; SWE-Smith [48] generates synthetic instances; SWE-Gym [32] curates runnable training instances; and SWE-Bench-Pro [25] targets harder tasks. Other variants, including SWE-PolyBench [35], SWE-Perf [27], SWE-Bench++ [40], SWE-Evo [39], SWE-Fixer [45], SWE-Flow [53], SWE-Universe [22], and SWE-Lego [37], extend the paradigm along other dimensions.
Benchmark Quality and Reliability. Benchmark reliability is a longstanding concern, with prior work highlighting test oracle insufficiency [42, 51], dataset contamination [14], and solution leakage [15]. SWE-ABS [50] strengthens test suites adversarially, while SPICE [30] automates labeling for SWE-bench-style datasets.
ComparisonwithOpenAI'sAnalysis. OpenAI's SWE-bench analysis [14] focuses on contamination and test coverage. This overlaps with parts of our taxonomy, such as PR Scope Creep, but not the construction-level root cause: a linked PR may not be intended to fix only the linked issue. Our taxonomy also covers cases beyond test coverage, such as defective PRs used as gold patches.
Comparison with SPICE. SPICE [30] follows the SWE-bench Verified annotation standard, prompting LLMs to transfer its quality criteria to SWE-Gym. In contrast, PaiChecker audits SWE-bench Verified itself and labels a more fundamental construction dimension. We compare PaiChecker with SPICE [30] through both quantitative and qualitative studies. (1) Quantitative comparison. We compare on the 644 instances whose instance IDs appear in both SPICE outputs and our annotations. On this overlap, SPICE flags 143 as problematic and PaiChecker flags 281 as misaligned, with 78 overlapping cases, 65 SPICE-only cases, and 203 PaiChecker-only cases. (2) Qualitative comparison. dask__dask-7305 is detected only by PaiChecker: the gold PR fixes a bug but introduces a regression, which PaiChecker flags as DP; SPICE misses it because a clear issue and matching tests obscure the weakened oracle. dask__dask-6862 is detected only by SPICE: the issue proposes get_if_none , and the PR implements the same semantics via override_with ; SPICE flags poor scoping due to API differences, while PaiChecker identifies no misalignment. conan-io__conan-16028 is flagged by both: the issue requests optional Git URL hiding, but the PR adds unrelated C-standard utilities; PaiChecker labels it SC, SPICE labels it poorly scoped tests.

Section: 9 Conclusion

This paper identifies PR-Issue misalignment as a systematic construction-level problem in SWE-bench-like benchmarks that directly undermines evaluation fairness and reliability. Manual analysis of all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances reveals 13.6% misalign- ment across five patterns and 11 fine-grained scenarios. To enable scalable de- tection, we propose PaiChecker, a three-phase multi-agent checker combining pattern-specific detection, beyond-taxonomy synthesis, and code validation. Evaluated on SWE-Gym and SWEbench Multilingual, PaiChecker reaches up to 92.12% and 91.67% accuracy, respectively.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 3.1 Phase I: Specific Misalignment Identification

In this subsection, we describe Phase I, which detects the five misalignment patterns using three parallel subagents, each focused on distinct reasoning: the Issue Analyzer targets Incomplete Specification (IS), primarily drawing on issue-side artifacts; the PR Scope Analyzer targets PR Scope Creep (SC) and Unspecified Literal (UL) through issue-versus-PR scope comparison; and the PR Connection Analyzer targets Defective PR (DP) and Follow-up PR (FP) through temporal cross-PR reasoning. This grouping keeps each subagent's context compact and reasoning focused. All three produce a uniform structured output: (i) a judgment per target pattern, (ii) supporting evidence for text-level self-correction, and (iii) suspicious clues -anomalies outside the subagent's target patterns that support beyond-taxonomy generalization.
3.1.1 Issue Analyzer. The Issue Analyzer operationalizes IS detection by comparing the issue description against its discussion thread. As mentioned in Section 2.2.1: a well-formed bug report comprises three key components: reproduction code, actual behavior, and expected behavior. Based on this, the subagent performs two checks.
First, whether the issue is incomplete: it identifies whether a maintainer explicitly requests the reporter to supplement any of these components, grounding the judgment in community consensus rather than subjective assessment. Second, whether the issue has been redefined: it checks whether any of these components differs between the original description and the discussion; a change in any component signals that the addressed problem has shifted.
3.1.2 PR Scope Analyzer. The PR Scope Analyzer detects SC and UL in a unified pass. Both patterns require establishing the issue's requested scope as a baseline and checking whether the PR exceeds it, so a single subagent establishes the baseline once and verifies both patterns together. This subagent receives the issue description as scope baseline, PR-side text for what the PR claims to deliver, and both patches for UL detection.
Following the text-driven, code-validation principle, SC is triggered only when PR-side textual artifacts explicitly claim work beyond the issue's scope. UL is triggered when all three conditions hold: (1) the test patch asserts a hardcoded literal ( e.g. a string, number, or exception message); (2) the literal is newly added in the code patch as a fixed constant, rather than read from existing metadata; and (3) it does not appear verbatim in the issue description.
3.1.3 PR Connection Analyzer. The PR Connection Analyzer detects DP and FP, both involve temporal relationships between the current PR and other PRs for the same issue. Tracing such crossPR dependency chains requires information beyond the current instance's artifacts, so we equip this subagent with GitHub API access to actively search for and retrieve related PRs.
PaiChecker : Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks
ASE '26, October 12-16, 2026, Munich, Germany
For DP detection, the agent searches for PRs merged after the current one that still address the same issue. Each candidate is verified for merge status to distinguish corrective follow-ups from unrelated references. For FP detection, the agent searches for earlier merged PRs that partially addressed the same issue, checking whether the current PR is a supplementary contribution rather than an independent fix, based on merge chronology and follow-up language in PR descriptions.

PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks

Section: 4.3 Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate PR-Issue misalignment detection from two complementary perspectives: (1) a binary classification task that judges whether an instance is aligned or misaligned, and (2) a multilabel classification task that identifies the specific misalignment patterns, where an instance may exhibit multiple patterns simultaneously. Accordingly, we adopt the following metrics:
Binary Detection. We measure accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 for the binary detection task.
Multi-Class Categorization. Exact Match (EM) serves as the primary metric, requiring the predicted label set to exactly match the ground truth. We supplement EM with macro-averaged accuracy, precision, recall, and F1. For per-label analysis, we report only F1 due to space constraints; F1 provides a balanced measure of precision and recall, making it sufficient for diagnostic purposes.

Section: 4.4 Backbone LLMs

We evaluate PaiChecker and baselines across four state-of-the-art LLM backbones, including three closed-source models GPT-5.3Codex [31], Claude-Sonnet-4.6 [16], Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview [26], and one open-sourced model Qwen-3.5-Plus [34]. All models were accessed through their respective APIs.

testCases.input: What are the defining characteristics and constraints of ILP-GT in voter interval contexts?
testCases.actualOutput:
In the context of Voter Interval (VI) preferences, the Integer Linear Program for Generalized Thiele (ILP-GT) is defined with specific characteristics and constraints that facilitate its solution. The VI property allows voters to be ordered such that each candidate is approved by a consecutive segment of voters. This structure is crucial for formulating the ILP-GT effectively.

The ILP-GT is designed to maximize voter satisfaction while selecting a committee of candidates. The formulation includes variables that track both the selection of candidates and the satisfaction levels of voters. Specifically, the variables \(y_c\) indicate selected candidates, while \(x_{v,i}\) tracks the satisfaction levels of voters for each candidate. The objective function is structured to ensure that the highest available values in a Thiele sequence are chosen, which is essential for achieving optimal outcomes under the voting rules [1].

One significant constraint in the VI context is that each candidate is supported by exactly two voters. This leads to a modification of the ILP-GT formulation, where the responsibility for enforcing the committee size is shifted from the candidate selection variables \(y_c\) to the voter satisfaction variables \(x_{v,i}\). This adjustment results in a constraint matrix that can be classified as a generalized matching matrix, which is solvable in polynomial time [2].

However, the challenge arises from the fact that while the transpose of the approval profile matrix may satisfy the consecutive ones property, appending an all-ones row can disrupt this property, leading to non-total unimodularity (TU) in certain cases. This non-TU condition complicates the polynomial-time solvability of the ILP-GT when dealing with VI preferences [1][3].

In summary, the defining characteristics of ILP-GT in the VI context include the structured approval profile of voters, the modification of constraints to accommodate the two-voter support per candidate, and the implications of total unimodularity on the solvability of the program.
testCases.expectedOutput:
ILP-GT (Integer Linear Programming for Generalized Thiele) in voter interval contexts is characterized by the following defining features and constraints:

1. **Approval Profiles**: The approval profile can be either Condorcet Interval (CI) or Voter Interval (VI). CI profiles maintain total unimodularity (TU), allowing for polynomial-time solutions, while VI profiles may not preserve TU when an all-ones row is appended.

2. **Variables**: The model includes variables \(y_c\) that indicate selected candidates and \(x_{v,i}\) that track voter satisfaction levels.

3. **Constraints**: The formulation includes constraints that ensure the selection of candidates aligns with voter approvals. In the case of CI, the constraints maintain the consecutive ones property, while for VI, this property may be lost, complicating the solution.

4. **Committee Size**: The original constraint ensuring exactly \(k\) candidates are selected is modified to shift responsibility to the voter satisfaction variables, ensuring that each candidate selected corresponds to two approving voters.

5. **Generalized Matching Matrix**: The modified ILP-GT formulation results in a generalized matching matrix, which allows for polynomial-time solvability under specific conditions regarding the coefficients of the constraint matrix.

6. **FPT Parameterization**: The problem is FPT (Fixed Parameter Tractable) parameterized by \( \Delta C + \Delta V \), indicating that it can be solved efficiently when the parameters related to candidate and voter diversity are bounded.

These characteristics and constraints define how ILP-GT operates within the voter interval context, influencing both its complexity and solvability.

Algorithms for Structured Elections under Thiele Voting Rules

Section: 1 Introduction Multi-winner elections based on approval ballots are used in many settings, such as recommendation systems, committee selection, and blockchain [SFL16, LS23, BBC + 24], where every voter expresses its preferences as a subset of candidates it approves of. A central family of voting rules for such applications are Thiele rules [Thi95], which include Proportional Approval Voting (PAV) as a prominent member [AGG + 15]. These rules balance diversity, proportionality, and excellence in the selected committee, depending on the specific Thiele rule used [LS21]. For instance, ChamberlinCourant Approval Voting (CC) [CC83] promotes diversity by ensuring broad representation; PAV aims for proportional representation, satisfying strong proportionality axioms like EJR+ [BP23]; Multi-winner Approval Voting focuses on excellence by selecting the most approved candidates. However, computing a winning committee under Thiele rules is computationally challenging. In fact, finding a winning committee under any non-trivial Thiele rule (i.e., every rule except for Multi-winner Approval Voting) is NP-hard. For CC and PAV, the problems remain NP-hard even ∗ A conference version of this work appeared in AAAI 2026 [LS26]. Krzysztof Sornat AGH University, Poland sornat@agh.edu.pl under very restricted conditions where each candidate is approved by exactly 3 voters and each voter approves exactly 2 candidates [AGG + 15, SFL16]. 1 In the CI domain, candidates can be ordered so that each voter's approval set forms a contiguous interval. CI captures scenarios where candidates are linearly ordered, e.g. by ideology or location, and each voter is focused on a specific region of the spectrum. One key advantage of CI is that it allows the winner determination problem for all Thiele rules to be solved efficiently. It is by using an integer linear programming formulation that admits a totally unimodular constraint matrix, which are known to be solvable in polynomial time [Pet18, PL20]. To better understand and overcome this computational hardness, a natural direction is to restrict the input domain. Such restrictions often enable polynomial-time algorithms for otherwise intractable rules, and this approach has been particularly fruitful in approval-based committee elections. Two central restricted domains for approval ballots are the Candidate Interval (CI) and the Voter Interval (VI) domains [ELP17, ELP25]. The VI domain, in contrast, imposes structure on the voters rather than on the candidates. Here, voters can be ordered so that each candidate is approved by a consecutive segment of voters. This domain models scenarios where voters are structured by demographic or socioeconomic features such as age, income, or education level, and candidates appeal to specific groups, e.g. young voters, low-income households, or university-educated individuals. The VI domain has received significant attention [ELP17, ELP25] and, consequently, for several voting rules, such as CC, Monroe's and Minimax Approval Voting polynomial-time winner-determination algorithms for VI elections are known [BSU13, LG16]. Yet, for most Thiele rules, and PAV in particular, the computational complexity of winner determination on VI remains a prominent open question [ELP17, Pet18, GBSF21, LS23, ELP25]. Despite the dual nature of the VI and CI domains, the techniques used for CI do not translate to VI. In particular, the constraint matrix of the integer linear programming formulation is not totally unimodular anymore under VI preferences and, thus, it is not clear whether this problem can be solved in polynomial time or not. This motivates a search for new structural results and algorithmic techniques. Structural Results. This work takes a new approach to understand the computational complexity of Thiele rules by studying the structure of winning committees. Instead of considering candidates in isolation, we examine how shared support among voters constrains the possible combinations of candidates in a winning committee. testCases.input: How does the total unimodularity of ILP-GT's constraint matrix influence CI approval profiles?
testCases.actualOutput:
The total unimodularity (TU) of the constraint matrix in the Integer Linear Programming formulation for Generalized Thiele (ILP-GT) plays a crucial role in efficiently solving the winner determination problem for Candidate Interval (CI) approval profiles. When the approval profile is classified as CI, the constraint matrix of ILP-GT retains the TU property, which allows for the identification of optimal solutions in polynomial time.

Specifically, Peters [Pet18] demonstrated that when an approval profile is CI, the constraint matrix exhibits the consecutive one property, a characteristic that is essential for total unimodularity. This property ensures that any integer linear program with a TU constraint matrix can be solved efficiently, as it allows for the application of polynomial-time algorithms. The implication is that for CI profiles, the structure of voter approvals can be leveraged to simplify the computational complexity of determining winning committees under Thiele rules.

In contrast, when the approval profile is classified as Voter Interval (VI), the total unimodularity may not be preserved, which complicates the problem significantly. The authors note that while the transpose of the approval matrix may satisfy the consecutive one property, appending an all-ones row can disrupt this property, leading to a non-TU matrix. This distinction highlights the computational advantages of CI profiles over VI profiles in the context of Thiele voting rules [1. arXiv:2607.28575v1].

In summary, the total unimodularity of ILP-GT's constraint matrix under CI profiles facilitates polynomial-time solutions, making it a powerful tool for efficiently determining winning committees in structured elections.

Section: 1 Introduction Multi-winner elections based on approval ballots are used in many settings, such as recommendation systems, committee selection, and blockchain [SFL16, LS23, BBC + 24], where every voter expresses its preferences as a subset of candidates it approves of. A central family of voting rules for such applications are Thiele rules [Thi95], which include Proportional Approval Voting (PAV) as a prominent member [AGG + 15]. These rules balance diversity, proportionality, and excellence in the selected committee, depending on the specific Thiele rule used [LS21]. For instance, ChamberlinCourant Approval Voting (CC) [CC83] promotes diversity by ensuring broad representation; PAV aims for proportional representation, satisfying strong proportionality axioms like EJR+ [BP23]; Multi-winner Approval Voting focuses on excellence by selecting the most approved candidates. However, computing a winning committee under Thiele rules is computationally challenging. In fact, finding a winning committee under any non-trivial Thiele rule (i.e., every rule except for Multi-winner Approval Voting) is NP-hard. For CC and PAV, the problems remain NP-hard even ∗ A conference version of this work appeared in AAAI 2026 [LS26]. Krzysztof Sornat AGH University, Poland sornat@agh.edu.pl under very restricted conditions where each candidate is approved by exactly 3 voters and each voter approves exactly 2 candidates [AGG + 15, SFL16]. 1 In the CI domain, candidates can be ordered so that each voter's approval set forms a contiguous interval. CI captures scenarios where candidates are linearly ordered, e.g. by ideology or location, and each voter is focused on a specific region of the spectrum. One key advantage of CI is that it allows the winner determination problem for all Thiele rules to be solved efficiently. It is by using an integer linear programming formulation that admits a totally unimodular constraint matrix, which are known to be solvable in polynomial time [Pet18, PL20]. To better understand and overcome this computational hardness, a natural direction is to restrict the input domain. Such restrictions often enable polynomial-time algorithms for otherwise intractable rules, and this approach has been particularly fruitful in approval-based committee elections. Two central restricted domains for approval ballots are the Candidate Interval (CI) and the Voter Interval (VI) domains [ELP17, ELP25]. The VI domain, in contrast, imposes structure on the voters rather than on the candidates. Here, voters can be ordered so that each candidate is approved by a consecutive segment of voters. This domain models scenarios where voters are structured by demographic or socioeconomic features such as age, income, or education level, and candidates appeal to specific groups, e.g. young voters, low-income households, or university-educated individuals. The VI domain has received significant attention [ELP17, ELP25] and, consequently, for several voting rules, such as CC, Monroe's and Minimax Approval Voting polynomial-time winner-determination algorithms for VI elections are known [BSU13, LG16]. Yet, for most Thiele rules, and PAV in particular, the computational complexity of winner determination on VI remains a prominent open question [ELP17, Pet18, GBSF21, LS23, ELP25]. Despite the dual nature of the VI and CI domains, the techniques used for CI do not translate to VI. In particular, the constraint matrix of the integer linear programming formulation is not totally unimodular anymore under VI preferences and, thus, it is not clear whether this problem can be solved in polynomial time or not. This work takes a new approach to understand the computational complexity of Thiele rules by studying the structure of winning committees. Instead of considering candidates in isolation, we examine how shared support among voters constrains the possible combinations of candidates in a winning committee. We provide a structural characterization of optimal committees under Thiele rules based on a dominance relation among candidates. Specifically, a candidate c is said to dominate another candidate d if the set of supporters of c strictly contains that of d . This induces a hierarchy of dominancy levels where candidates within the same level do not dominate one another and each is dominated by some candidate in a higher level. We show that there always exists a winning committee that is non-dominated , meaning that no member is dominated by any candidate outside the committee. These structural insights apply to general approval profiles and are of independent interest, offering new theoretical tools for analyzing and determining winners under Thiele rules. Practically, this structure can guide the development of more efficient algorithms and heuristics. Theoretically, it offers a new perspective on the open question of whether winner determination under PAV is polynomial-time solvable on VI. 2 Algorithmic Results. We show that our structural insights are particularly effective when combined with the VI property: candidates of a VI instance can be partitioned into parts such that candidates within a part influence only a limited number of voters. This allows to design a dynamic program over a sequence of such parts, exploiting the limited interaction. As a result, we obtain an FPT algorithm for PAV and, more generally, for any Thiele rule, when parameterized by two parameters combined: the maximum number of approvals received by a candidate, and the maximum number of approvals in a vote. Notably, the same parameterization is para-NP-hard in the general (unstructured) case-that is, the problem remains NP-hard even when both parameters are constants. This contrast highlights the algorithmic power of our structural approach and provides substantial progress toward resolving the open question on the complexity of PAV in the VI domain [ELP17, Pet18, LS23, ELP25]. Beyond the VI setting, we further contribute to understanding tractable cases for Thiele rules by resolving two open problems posed by Yang and Wang [YW18, YW23], originally asked for PAV: (1) we provide a polynomial-time algorithm for instances where each candidate is approved by at most two voters, based on a proper integer linear programming formulation; and (2) we give an FPT algorithm parameterized by the total score of a winning committee, employing combinatorial tools like color-coding and splitters.
